source: Uganda Christian University Academic Research Manual, revised April 2018
note: The manual is a general guide: faculties may document their own variations (manual, About this manual and §1.1). Pages cited are the manual's printed page numbers (add seven for the PDF page). Only proposal rules are here: concept-paper (§1.4) and final-report rules (§4-§5.8) do not apply to a proposal.

APA7.label: APA 7th edition (if your faculty uses it)
APA7.source: §1.6, p. 5: faculties may communicate their own style

words_per_page_source: §1.7, p. 6 (double spacing, 1 inch margins, Trebuchet MS 12)

items: Glossary of Terms and Acronyms (where applicable)
preliminary_pages.title_page: The intended title, the candidate's name and student number, the academic programme, the proposed supervisor and the date of submission.

rules.requirement: The proposal is written in the future tense, since it precedes the research.
rules.interpretation: PaperAid applies this to the planned study only; published studies and established facts keep their natural tense.

rules.requirement: Three chapters or sections: General Introduction, Literature Review and Methodology. They may run continuously; chapter numbers are optional.
A reference list at the end lists every work referred to in the text, in APA style.
State the main objective and the specific objectives, each in a single sentence; two to five specific objectives are generally sufficient.

Research questions, hypotheses or propositions that are precise and not obvious; two to five are generally sufficient. Hypotheses only where inferential statistical testing is planned, stated as null and alternative.
A work plan or timeline; a budget is optional.
Proposals whose methods may affect participants' privacy or well-being are approved by the Research Ethics Committee before any data are collected.
rules.interpretation: PaperAid describes the planned safeguards and the approval to be sought; it never states that approval has been obtained.

rules.requirement: Studies using purely secondary data, projects and extended essays may not follow the full format; the faculty's own format applies.
Faculties may set their own variations; students check with their faculty office for supplementary guidelines.
rules.source: About this manual, p. i; §1.1, p. 1

chapters.title: General Introduction
chapters.purpose: The supervisor or committee should have no difficulty understanding the objective of the study and why it is important.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.brief: What the chapter covers, in a few sentences.

sections.heading: Background to the Study
sections.brief: Historical, theoretical, conceptual and contextual background, moving from broad to narrow, defining the key concepts and building the case for the problem statement.

sections.heading: Statement of the Problem
sections.brief: The central problem stated clearly: the need for research, the gap in knowledge or practice it fills, and why it matters now.

sections.heading: Purpose of the Study
sections.brief: The general objective in one or two sentences, aligned to the problem.

sections.heading: Objectives of the Study
sections.brief: The specific objectives from the approved plan, each one sentence, going beyond 'to study' to analysis.

sections.heading: Research Questions
sections.brief: The research questions (or hypotheses, or propositions) from the approved plan, aligned one to one with the objectives.

sections.heading: Scope of the Study
sections.brief: Geographical, time and content scope.

sections.heading: Justification of the Study
sections.brief: Why the study is being undertaken: convincing and brief. Must differ from significance.

sections.heading: Significance of the Study
sections.brief: Its importance to the field, the problem or policy, and its expected contribution to knowledge. Must differ from justification.

sections.heading: Conceptual Framework
sections.brief: The theory or theories applied and the conceptual framework: independent, dependent and any intervening variables and how they relate.

sections.heading: Organisation of the Proposal
sections.brief: A short synopsis of the three chapters.

chapters.title: Literature Review
chapters.purpose: A focused, evaluative examination of the literature that leads the reader to the research questions and the gap the study fills.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.brief: What the review covers and how it is organised.

sections.heading: Theoretical Review
sections.brief: The theory applied to the problem, not merely described: critical analysis, similarities and differences between views.

sections.heading: Empirical Review
sections.brief: One sub-section per specific objective: approaches, analyses, findings and conclusions of prior studies, analysed critically rather than summarised study by study.

sections.heading: Summary and Research Gap
sections.brief: What is known, what is contested and the gap this study addresses.

chapters.title: Methodology
chapters.purpose: An explicit description of how the study will be conducted, so the reader can judge whether the results will be reliable and valid, and could replicate it.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.brief: What the chapter covers.

sections.heading: Research Design
sections.brief: The design and the rationale for choosing it.

sections.heading: Area of Study
sections.brief: Where the study will take place and why that area suits the problem.

sections.heading: Sources of Information
sections.brief: Primary and secondary data sources.

sections.heading: Study Population
sections.brief: The target population and why it is appropriate.

sections.heading: Sample Size and Sampling Techniques
sections.brief: How the sample size will be determined (formula and assumptions), the sampling procedure, and inclusion and exclusion criteria. Probability sampling for quantitative studies; non-probability for qualitative.

sections.heading: Variables and Measurement
sections.brief: Dependent and independent variables, how each will be measured and its level of measurement (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio).

sections.heading: Data Collection Procedure
sections.brief: Step by step, how data will be collected.

sections.heading: Data Collection Instruments
sections.brief: The tools (questionnaire, interview guide, observation checklist, equipment) and why they suit the objectives.

sections.heading: Quality Control
sections.brief: How validity and reliability of the instruments will be ensured, including any pilot or pre-test.

sections.heading: Data Processing and Analysis
sections.brief: How data will be cleaned and analysed, the method for each objective, and any software.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.brief: Confidentiality, consent, assent, anonymity and approval by the Research Ethics Committee where required.

sections.heading: Anticipated Methodological Constraints
sections.brief: Expected limits of the methods and how they will be handled.

sections.heading: Work Plan
sections.brief: A timeline of the study's activities, month by month, as a table.

vetting.source: Form for vetting proposals and detailed guidelines for assessment, Appendix C §7.3.1, pp. 50-52
vetting.note: The form gives 20, 15 and 15 marks (total 50) while the guidelines label them as percentages; PaperAid uses the questions as a checklist and gives no marks.

1.question: Does the background go sufficiently from broad to narrow on the topic?
Does the background make a case for the problem statement?
Does the problem statement clearly state the problem and the gap in scholarly knowledge the research will fill?
Is the purpose clearly stated, with objectives that support it and go beyond 'study' to higher-level research (analysis)?
Is the purpose aligned to the research problem, questions and/or hypotheses?
Is there a primary research question with aligned questions supporting it?
Is there a clear difference between justification and significance?
Does the content reflect quality organisation and flow?
Are grammar, punctuation and word choice accurate?
Is all content related to the topic?
Is a conceptual or theoretical framework given?

2.question: Are there a minimum of 30 quality references?
2.note: From the School of Research and Postgraduate Studies' proposal vetting guidelines; check whether your programme applies it.

2.question: Is there evidence of quoting original sources rather than sources cited within prior research?
Is there a balance of source types (data and prior research)?
Is there a balance of sources (more than one source drives each part)?
Does the writing engage with and analyse the literature, rather than show what was read?
Do the sources align with the topic, purpose, research questions and objectives?
Are references missing that should be included to support the objectives and purpose?
Are there transitions within and between paragraphs?
Is all content related to the topic?
Is there appropriate grammar, punctuation and word choice?
Is the literature up to date for this field? (The guidelines leave this to the faculty and the research; foundational theory is not out of date.)
Is the research gap clear and articulate, showing the contribution of the study?
Is the flow of information logical?

3.question: Is the methodology aligned with the research?
Is the methodology appropriate and adequate for the research task?
Are the methods consistent with the chosen methodology?
Are the study design and its rationale appropriate?
Are inclusion and exclusion criteria clearly stated?
Are ethical considerations during data collection addressed?
Are the reliability and validity of the research tools addressed?
Is the data analysis process clearly described?
